components/actions.title: Actions
components/actions.text: Actions FilledButton, TonalButton, OutlinedButton, TextButton Four levels of emphasis, from the screen's main action to the least important. Each takes an icon (or "" ) and a label, and returns true when touched. padded(look, func() { look.FilledButton("check", "Save") // the main action of the screen look.TonalButton("lightbulb", "Light it") // important, but not the main one look.OutlinedButton("share-2", "Share") // secondary look.TextButton("", "Not now") // the least important: in dialogs, beside others }) Save filled, Light it tonal, Share outlined, Not now as text One filled button per screen at most. Dialogs use text buttons (the Dialog piece does it for you). NamedIconButton, IconButton, RoundButton, SplitButton A round 48-pixel target with an icon. NamedIconButton(icon, name) gives TalkBack a name for it: use it always, unless the icon's meaning is in words beside it ( IconButton(icon) ). RoundButton(icon, size, primary) floats over a map or a scene. SplitButton joins a main action to an arrow opening its other choices, and tells which half was touched. padded(look, func() { look.Context.Row(func() { look.NamedIconButton("heart", "Favourite") // a name for TalkBack look.NamedIconButton("share-2", "Share") look.Context.Spacer() look.RoundButton("locate", 48, false) // over a map: centre on me look.RoundButton("plus", 48, true) }) look.Context.Row(func() { if action, more := look.SplitButton("send", "Send"); action { // send now } else if more { // open the other ways of sending } }) }) A heart and share icons, two round buttons, and Send split from its arrow FloatingButton and ExtendedFloatingButton The floating action button: the screen's one main action (write, add), at the bottom end, over the content. The extended one says its action in words: use it while the screen is at rest, as on a list's first screen. look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, nil) // the list look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(16), Gap: 16, AlignX: ui.End}, func() { look.FloatingButton("pencil") // the screen's one main action look.ExtendedFloatingButton("plus", "New lighthouse") // the same, with its words }) A pencil floating button and an extended New lighthouse button FloatingMenu(name, &menu) opens into a few related actions stacked above it, its icon turning into a cross; it returns the action touched, or -1. menu.Label names it for TalkBack. ButtonGroup and FloatingToolbar ButtonGroup (Material 3 Expressive's connected buttons) chooses one of a few, the chosen one filled and rounded out. FloatingToolbar is a pill of actions floating at the bottom, for what is done to the content on show; it returns the index of the tool touched, or -1, and TalkBack reads each tool's label. padded(look, func() { look.ButtonGroup("view", []string{"Day", "Week", "Month"}, &view) }) look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, nil) switch look.FloatingToolbar("tools", []material.Destination{ {Icon: "pencil", Label: "Edit"}, {Icon: "share-2", Label: "Share"}, {Icon: "trash-2", Label: "Remove"}, }, 16) { case 0: // edit case 1: // share case 2: // remove } Day, Week and Month with Week chosen, and a floating toolbar with edit, share and remove ← Navigation · Selection →

components/components.title: Components
components/components.text: Components Every Material piece of material , one by one: when to use it, concrete cases with their code, how it behaves under a finger and with TalkBack. Each case is a real program's code, and the pictures are captures of it in a phone-sized window. The pieces shows them all at a glance; this is the page to read when using one. The cases assume the usual frame: look is the material.Look made in it ( material.New(context, scheme) ), and variables such as lit or place belong to your program and live between frames. padded stands for a column with the screen's margins: func padded(look material.Look, content func()) { look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(16), Gap: 12}, content) } Page Pieces Navigation TopAppBar , NavigationBar , NavigationRail , NavigationDrawer , Tabs , Screens Actions FilledButton , TonalButton , OutlinedButton , TextButton , IconButton , NamedIconButton , RoundButton , SplitButton , FloatingButton , ExtendedFloatingButton , FloatingMenu , ButtonGroup , FloatingToolbar Selection Switch , Checkbox , RadioButton , SegmentedButtons , Slider , FilterChip , InputChip , AssistChip , Tag Inputs TextField , Dropdown , SearchBar , SearchView Containment ListItem , ExpandableItem , Card , OutlinedCard , ElevatedCard , Avatar , Banner , SectionTitle , Divider Overlays Dialog , BottomSheet , StandardSheet , SideSheet , Snackbar , Menu Pickers DatePicker , TimePicker Progress LoadingIndicator , CircularProgress , WavyProgress , LinearProgress , Skeleton Gestures Carousel , MultiBrowseCarousel , TabPager , PullToRefresh , SwipeToDismiss , LongPressed , Stick Rules every piece follows Pieces that can be touched return true in the frame they are touched ; pieces that edit a value take a pointer to it. Overlays that ask return a material.Answer . A piece is told apart by its name (its label, its icon, or a name given). Rows that repeat get a scope each: look.Context.Push(name) … look.Context.Pop() . Targets are at least 48 pixels , as Material asks. A finger has no hover: pieces change only while pressed. Colours come from the scheme ( look.Scheme.OnSurface , ErrorContainer …), so the dark theme and the wallpaper's colours follow. Every piece is read by TalkBack ; icon buttons need a name ( NamedIconButton ). ← Documentation

components/containment.title: Containment
components/containment.text: Containment ListItem A list row: an icon in a round avatar (or a photo, Picture ), a headline, a supporting line, and Trailing for what goes at its end (a switch, an icon button, a tag). It returns true when touched. Selected tints it and puts a tick in the avatar's place, for rows chosen with a long press. look.SectionTitle("On the coast") names := []string{"North Point", "Harbour Mole", "South Reef"} places := []string{"On the northern cliffs", "At the harbour's mouth", "On a rock off the reef"} for index, name := range names { look.Context.Push(name) // rows repeat: a scope each if look.ListItem("row", material.Item{Icon: "lighthouse", Headline: name, Supporting: places[index], Trailing: func() { look.Switch("lit", &lit[index]) }}) { // open its screen } look.Context.Pop() } look.Divider() look.ListItem("chosen", material.Item{Icon: "lighthouse", Headline: "East Cape", Selected: true}) // chosen with a long press On the coast, three lighthouses with switches, a line, and East Cape chosen with a tick Touching the switch at its end does not touch the row. For photos, decode a draw2d.Image once and pass it as Picture . ExpandableItem A row that unfolds to show more under it, its chevron turning: questions and answers, details. questions := []string{"When is the lamp lit?", "Can it be visited?"} answers := []string{"From sunset to sunrise, and in fog.", "On summer weekends."} for index, question := range questions { look.ExpandableItem(fmt.Sprint("question ", index), material.Item{Headline: question}, &open[index], func() { look.Paragraph(answers[index], 14, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurfaceVariant) }) } When is the lamp lit? open with its answer, Can it be visited? closed Card, OutlinedCard, ElevatedCard, Avatar Containers for one subject. Filled on a plain screen, outlined beside other cards, elevated over a map or a scene. Avatar(name, icon, tint, size) draws a person's initials (or an icon) in a circle; PictureAvatar(picture, size) a photo. padded(look, func() { look.Card(func() { // filled: on a plain screen look.Text("North Point", 16, draw2d.Medium, look.Scheme.OnSurface) look.Text("Lit, 18 nautical miles", 14, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurfaceVariant) }) look.OutlinedCard(func() { // drawn by its border: beside other cards look.Context.Row(func() { look.Avatar("Ana Keeper", "", draw2d.Color{}, 40) // initials in a circle look.Text("Ana Keeper is on duty", 14, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurface) }) }) look.ElevatedCard(func() { // raised: over a map or a scene look.Text("Fog warning tonight", 14, draw2d.Medium, look.Scheme.OnSurface) }) }) A filled card, an outlined card with AK initials, and a raised card Banner A message across the top that stays until acted on: no connection, an update. It returns the index of the action touched, or -1. if shown { switch look.Banner("wifi-off", "The positions were last brought up to date a week ago.", "Dismiss", "Refresh") { case 0: shown = false case 1: shown = false // and refresh } } look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, nil) A banner with a no-wifi icon, a message, and Dismiss and Refresh For a note that goes by itself, use a Snackbar . SectionTitle, Heading, Divider, Text, Paragraph A small heading over a list's rows; a heading for content with its own margins; a line between groups; one line of text; and text that breaks into lines at the width it has ( Paragraph , the only piece that wraps). ← Inputs · Overlays →

components/gestures.title: Gestures
components/gestures.text: Gestures A finger is followed from where it comes down; the way it goes first decides who takes it (a list for up and down, the innermost sideways piece for sideways), so these pieces nest freely. Carousel and MultiBrowseCarousel A row of tiles slid sideways, gliding on and settling at a tile. The program keeps a material.Carousel . CarouselItem(height, tint, icon, title) and CarouselPicture(picture, height, title) are ready tiles. MultiBrowseCarousel shows large tiles, then a medium and a small one, growing as they come in. places := []string{"Cliffs", "Harbour", "Reef", "Dunes", "Island"} tints := []draw2d.Color{draw2d.Hex("#b3d4e0"), draw2d.Hex("#c9e0b3"), draw2d.Hex("#e0cdb3"), draw2d.Hex("#e0b3c4"), draw2d.Hex("#c4b3e0")} look.SectionTitle("Places") look.Carousel("places", &carousel, len(places), 140, func(index int) { look.CarouselItem(160, tints[index], "map-pin", places[index]) }) Places, and tiles Cliffs, Harbour and Reef in a row TabPager Tabs over pages a finger swipes from side to side, the underline following them. The program keeps a material.Pager ; pager.Selected is the page on show. look.TabPager("pages", []string{"Today", "Tomorrow", "Week"}, &pager, func(index int) { padded(look, func() { look.Text(fmt.Sprint("Forecast for page ", index+1), 16, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurface) }) }) Today, Tomorrow and Week tabs, Today chosen, and its page PullToRefresh and SwipeToDismiss A list that refreshes when pulled past its top and let go (it returns true then; keep refreshing true until done), and rows a finger slides away (true when gone). if look.PullToRefresh("lights", refreshing, ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { for index := 0; index < len(names); index++ { look.Context.Push(names[index]) if look.SwipeToDismiss("swipe", func() { look.ListItem("row", material.Item{Icon: "lighthouse", Headline: names[index]}) }) { names = append(names[:index], names[index+1:]...) // swiped away index-- } look.Context.Pop() } }) { refreshing = true // pulled down and let go: refresh, then set it back to false } Three lighthouse rows in a list that can be pulled and swiped LongPressed Whether the piece drawn just before was held for half a second: the phone buzzes. A list starts choosing rows with it. touched := look.ListItem("row", material.Item{Headline: light.name, Selected: light.chosen}) switch { case look.LongPressed(): light.chosen = true // start choosing case touched && choosing: light.chosen = !light.chosen case touched: navigation.Go(light.name) } Stick An on-screen stick for walking or driving with a thumb. The finger that comes down on it holds it; stick.Forward and stick.Sideways go from -1 to 1. Other fingers stay free, to turn a view ( look.Context.Touches() , leaving out stick.Touching(touch) ). look.Stick("walk", &stick, 120) walker.Steer(stick.Forward, stick.Sideways, step) // go-renderer's camera.Walk ← Progress · Components

components/inputs.title: Inputs
components/inputs.text: Inputs TextField Material's text field, outlined or Filled , editing your string. material.Field says what goes round it: padded(look, func() { look.TextField("name", &name, material.Field{Label: "Name", MaxLength: 40, Counter: true}) look.TextField("range", &rangeText, material.Field{Label: "Range", Suffix: "nm", Supporting: "How far the light is seen"}) look.TextField("password", &password, material.Field{Label: "Keeper's password", Secret: true, Reveal: &reveal, Filled: true}) }) A Name field with 11/40, a Range field with nm and a hint, a filled password field with an eye Field Means Label , Placeholder Above the box; quiet in it while empty Supporting , Error A hint under it; an error instead, the box turned red MaxLength , Counter The most characters; a count under it Prefix , Suffix A currency, a unit, written in the box Secret , Reveal A password; with Reveal , an eye shows it while *Reveal is true Filled Material's filled field, for a form on a plain screen On a phone the keyboard comes up while it is typed in, suggests words and underlines the one it composes; a finger held on a word selects it, with handles and a bar to cut, copy and paste (in look.Words , the person's language). Saying what is wrong padded(look, func() { field := material.Field{Label: "Email", Placeholder: "keeper@example.com"} if email != "" && !validEmail(email) { field.Error = "That does not look like an email" } look.TextField("email", &email, field) }) An Email field in red with That does not look like an email Show the error once something was typed, not on an empty form. Dropdown Material's exposed dropdown: a box showing the choice that opens the choices under it. The program keeps a material.Dropdown , whose Selected is the choice. padded(look, func() { colours := []string{"White", "Red", "Green", "Amber"} if look.Dropdown("colour", "Light colour", colours, &dropdown) { // dropdown.Selected changed } }) Light colour: Red, in a box with an arrow SearchBar and SearchView SearchBar is a pill to search in, with a cross to empty it, above results the program filters. SearchView(name, placeholder, &search, content) is a pill that opens over the whole screen, ready to type in, with what the program finds under it; search.Query is what is typed and search.Active whether it is open. padded(look, func() { look.SearchBar("search", &text, "Search lighthouses") for _, name := range []string{"East Cape", "West Cape"} { // what matches text look.ListItem(name, material.Item{Icon: "lighthouse", Headline: name}) } }) A search pill with cape, and East Cape and West Cape under it ← Selection · Containment →

components/navigation.title: Navigation
components/navigation.text: Navigation TopAppBar The bar at the top of a screen, painted up under the status bar. It returns true when its back arrow is touched. look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "Lighthouses", Large: true}) // a screen's first level look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "North Point", Subtitle: "On the northern cliffs", Back: true, Actions: func() { look.NamedIconButton("share-2", "Share") look.NamedIconButton("pencil", "Edit") }}) look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "2 chosen", Back: true, Close: true, // a mode, left with the cross Actions: func() { look.NamedIconButton("trash-2", "Remove") }}) Three bars: a large Lighthouses title, North Point with a back arrow, a subtitle and two actions, and 2 chosen with a cross and a bin Case Use A destination's first screen Large: true : the title big under the bar. With Scrolled: look.Context.ScrollOffset("list") it shrinks into a small bar as the list goes up A screen gone to from another Back: true , and navigation.Back() when it returns true A mode, such as rows chosen Back: true, Close: true : a cross, and the count as the title Over a map or a 3D scene OverScene: true : see-through Actions go in Actions , usually NamedIconButton s; more than two or three go in a Menu . NavigationBar and NavigationRail Three to five destinations at the bottom, painted under the gesture bar. It edits the index of the destination chosen; show the screen with a switch . A Badge marks a destination with a count or, with "•" , a dot. places := []material.Destination{ {Icon: "lighthouse", Label: "Lights"}, {Icon: "map", Label: "Map"}, {Icon: "bell", Label: "Alerts", Badge: "3"}, // a count {Icon: "user", Label: "Me", Badge: "•"}, // a dot } look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, nil) // the screen above it look.NavigationBar(places, &place) A navigation bar with Lights chosen, Map, Alerts with a 3 and Me with a dot On a phone on its side ( look.Wide() ), draw NavigationRail(places, &place) down the left instead, with look.Body(true, …) . Lift floating things over the bar by material.NavigationBarHeight . NavigationDrawer Every destination in a drawer sliding in from the left: for more than five destinations, or ones seldom used. It returns true when it closes (a destination touched, the scrim, the back gesture). Open it from a menu icon in the top bar. look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "Lighthouses"}) places := []material.Destination{{Icon: "lighthouse", Label: "Lights"}, {Icon: "map", Label: "Map"}, {Icon: "bell", Label: "Alerts"}, {Icon: "settings", Label: "Settings"}} if open && look.NavigationDrawer("drawer", "Coast guard", places, &place) { open = false // a destination touched, the scrim touched, or the back gesture } The drawer open over a screen Tabs Primary tabs under the top bar, the underline sliding to the one chosen, for views of one thing (a lighthouse's overview, light and history). For tabs whose pages a finger swipes, use TabPager . look.Tabs("view", []string{"Overview", "Light", "History"}, &tab) padded(look, func() { switch tab { case 0: look.Text("North Point, on the northern cliffs", 16, 0, look.Scheme.OnSurface) case 1: look.Text("White, every five seconds", 16, 0, look.Scheme.OnSurface) case 2: look.Text("Lit for the first time long ago", 16, 0, look.Scheme.OnSurface) } }) Tabs Overview, Light and History, Light chosen, and its text Screens, Navigation, GoBack A stack of screens inside one destination: a list, then one row's screen, then a form. The program keeps a material.Navigation ; Go(name) opens a screen sliding in from the right, Back() returns, and look.Screens draws the one on top by its name ( "" is the first). look.Screens("lighthouses", &navigation, func(key string) { if key == "" { drawList(look) // its rows call navigation.Go(light.name) return } drawLighthouse(look, key) }) // last in the frame, after dialogs and sheets: if look.GoBack(&navigation) { return // the back gesture went back a screen } if look.Back() { … // anything else the back should do; nobody answering sends the app to the background } See the tutorial's lesson 2 for a whole app. ← Components · Actions →

components/overlays.title: Overlays
components/overlays.text: Overlays Draw overlays after the screen in the frame (a defer at the start of the frame does it), so they are on top and answer the back gesture first. Dialog A question over the dimmed screen. Show it while your program asks; it returns material.Open while waiting, then Confirmed or Dismissed (the other action, a touch outside, the back gesture) once. if asking { answer := look.Dialog("switch off", material.Dialog{Icon: "lightbulb-off", Title: "Switch every light off?", Text: "Ships will not see the coast until they are lit again.", Confirm: "Switch off", Dismiss: "Cancel"}) if answer == material.Confirmed { // switch them off } asking = answer == material.Open // Confirmed or Dismissed: it closes } Switch every light off? with an icon, a line, Cancel and Switch off Content adds more under the text (a field, choices). BottomSheet, StandardSheet, SideSheet Piece When BottomSheet(name, content) Choices or a short form rising from the bottom, the screen dimmed. Returns true when dragged down or dismissed StandardSheet(name, &sheet, peek, content) A sheet over the screen that does not dim it (a map's places): it rests low or expanded, dragged by its handle SideSheet(name, title, content) Filters or details sliding in from the end, with a title and a cross if open && look.BottomSheet("actions", func() { look.ListItem("share", material.Item{Icon: "share-2", Headline: "Share the chart"}) look.ListItem("copy", material.Item{Icon: "copy", Headline: "Copy the position"}) if look.ListItem("close", material.Item{Icon: "x", Headline: "Close"}) { open = false } }) { open = false // dragged down, the scrim touched, or the back gesture } Snackbar A short note at the bottom for a few seconds, with an action that undoes or follows what was just done. Keep one material.Snackbar , call Show(text, action, duration) when something happens, and draw it in every frame; it returns true when its action is touched. Set Above to material.NavigationBarHeight over a navigation bar. if first { // when something happens: here, at once notes.Show("North Point removed", "Undo", 5*time.Second) } look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, nil) if look.Snackbar(&notes) { // every frame // put it back } Menu A button (three dots, usually) that opens a list of choices under it; it returns the one chosen, or -1. TalkBack reads the button as "More options". look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "North Point", Actions: func() { switch look.Menu("ellipsis-vertical", []string{"Rename", "Duplicate", "Remove"}) { case 0: // rename case 1: // duplicate case 2: // remove } }}) A top bar with North Point and a three-dots menu ← Containment · Pickers →

components/pickers.title: Pickers
components/pickers.text: Pickers Both are dialogs: show them while choosing, and they answer Open , Confirmed or Dismissed . They edit a time.Time only when confirmed. The program keeps a picker struct while it is shown. DatePicker A day chosen a month at a time, with arrows to the months before and after. if open { switch look.DatePicker("inspection", &picker, &date) { case material.Confirmed: // date holds the day chosen open = false case material.Dismissed: open = false } } Select date, 21 June 2026, a month with the 21st chosen picker.Names (a material.DateNames ) gives the month and day names in another language. TimePicker Material's dial: the hours 1 to 12 round it and 13 to 00 inside, then the minutes; touched or dragged round. if open && look.TimePicker("light at", &picker, &date) != material.Open { open = false // Confirmed: date has the time chosen } Select time 21:30 on a dial with 21 chosen ← Overlays · Progress →

components/progress.title: Progress
components/progress.text: Progress padded(look, func() { look.Context.Row(func() { look.LoadingIndicator(48) // a short wait, nothing to measure look.ContainedLoadingIndicator(48) // the same on a round container look.CircularProgress(0.7, 48, false) look.CircularProgress(material.Indeterminate, 48, true) }) look.WavyProgress(0.6) // work being done, with a fraction look.LinearProgress(0.3) look.Skeleton(ui.Grow(), ui.Fixed(16), 4) // content still coming look.Skeleton(ui.Percent(0.6), ui.Fixed(16), 4) }) Two morphing loading shapes, a ring at 70 %, an arc, a wavy line, a straight line and two skeleton blocks Piece When LoadingIndicator(size) , ContainedLoadingIndicator(size) A short wait with nothing to measure: Expressive's shape that turns and morphs CircularProgress(fraction, size, wavy) Work with a fraction, in a small place; material.Indeterminate for an arc chasing round WavyProgress(fraction) , LinearProgress(fraction) Work with a fraction across the screen Skeleton(width, height, radius) Blocks standing in for content still coming, with a light crossing them Indicators ask for frames only while on screen; a screen without one sleeps. VideoPlayer(name, video, height) plays a film ( window.OpenVideo ) in a rounded box, touched to play or pause: see the pieces . ← Pickers · Gestures →

components/selection.title: Selection
components/selection.text: Selection Switch, Checkbox, RadioButton Piece When Switch(name, &on) A setting that takes effect at once; at the end of a row or a list item Checkbox(label, &on) One of several facts in a form, or rows to choose RadioButton(label, chosen) One of a few choices, all in sight; it returns true when touched, and the program chooses padded(look, func() { look.Context.Row(func() { look.Text("Lit", 16, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurface) look.Context.Spacer() look.Switch("lit", &lit) // takes effect at once }) look.Checkbox("Has a foghorn", &foghorn) // part of a form for index, name := range []string{"White", "Red", "Green"} { if look.RadioButton(name, colour == index) { // one of a few, all in sight colour = index } } }) Lit with a switch, an empty Has a foghorn checkbox, and White, Red and Green with White chosen TalkBack reads a switch as on or off, a checkbox as ticked, a radio button as chosen. SegmentedButtons and Slider Two to five short choices sharing a row, one chosen (units, a view); and a value between two ends, in steps. Write the value beside a slider when it matters. padded(look, func() { look.SegmentedButtons("units", []string{"Miles", "Kilometres"}, &units) look.Slider("volume", &volume, 0, 10, 1) look.Text(fmt.Sprintf("Foghorn volume %.0f", volume), 14, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurfaceVariant) }) Miles chosen beside Kilometres, a slider and Foghorn volume 6 Chips and tags Piece When FilterChip(label, selected) A filter on or off over a list; returns true when touched InputChip(label) Something entered (a tag, a person), with a cross: returns touched, removed AssistChip(icon, label) An action suggested beside the content Tag(text, ink, tint) A label in its own colours: a state, a count. It is not touched padded(look, func() { look.Context.Row(func() { // filters over a list if look.FilterChip("Lit", lit) { lit = !lit } if look.FilterChip("Stone", stone) { stone = !stone } }) look.Context.Row(func() { // what was entered, removable for index := 0; index < len(tags); index++ { if _, removed := look.InputChip(tags[index]); removed { tags = append(tags[:index], tags[index+1:]...) index-- } } }) look.Context.Row(func() { // suggested actions look.AssistChip("map-pin", "Show on the map") look.Tag("Needs repair", look.Scheme.OnErrorContainer, look.Scheme.ErrorContainer) }) }) Lit chosen and Stone filters, Listed and Painted removable chips, Show on the map and a red Needs repair tag ← Actions · Inputs →

getting-started.title: 🚀 Getting started

sections.text: Building against Go UI and Go Renderer

getting-started.text: 🚀 Getting started Two things for a Go UI program that should feel at home on a phone: material , pieces drawn the way Android's own applications are (Material Design 3, with Material 3 Expressive's newer pieces), and go-ui-apk , a tool that turns the program into an Android package. Neither needs Java, Gradle or Android Studio. The program stays an ordinary Go main package that calls Go UI's window.Run : on the desktop it opens a window, built for WebAssembly it draws in a web page, and on Android it is a shared library that Android's own NativeActivity loads (Go Renderer's android package). Using the pieces A program makes a material.Look in every frame, from the Go UI context and a colour scheme, and calls its pieces. Pieces that can be touched return true in the frame they are touched, as Go UI's own controls do; the ones that keep something between frames (a pager, a carousel, a snackbar, a picker) take a small struct of the program's. dark := window.SystemPrefersDark() scheme := material.System(dark) // the wallpaper's colours on Android 12 and later context.Theme = scheme.Theme(dark) look := material.New(context, scheme) look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "Lighthouses"}) if look.FilledButton("plus", "Add one") { … } look.NavigationBar(places, &screen) Sizes are Material's: targets of at least 48 pixels, bars 64 and 80 pixels tall, 16-pixel text. A finger has no hover, so pieces change only while pressed. Each piece takes the name Go UI tells it apart by (its label, its icon or a name given); rows that repeat get a scope each with context.Push , as in Go UI. material.UseRoboto() , before the window opens, draws every text in Roboto, Android's typeface. Building against Go UI and Go Renderer Go UI for Android builds against go-ui and go-renderer checked out beside it ( replace in go.mod ), until they publish versions with touches, insets, the wallpaper's palettes and the Android window. Then package it for a phone , and see every piece . ← All the documentation

guides/colours.title: 🎨 Colours
guides/colours.text: 🎨 Colours A Scheme holds Material's colour roles: the primary colour and the text on it, its container, the surface and the raised containers over it, the outlines, the error colours and the inverse ones. material.System(dark) takes the colours the phone made from its wallpaper (Android 12 and later, Material You), as the system's own applications do, and Material's baseline elsewhere (an older phone, the desktop, a browser). Call it in every frame: the colours change with the wallpaper. The roles are taken from Android's palettes as its own dynamic colours take them: the primary from the first accent palette, the containers from the second, the surfaces from the neutral ones; the error colours stay Material's. material.Baseline(dark) is Material's own purple scheme, always the same. material.FromColour(colour, dark) makes a whole scheme from one colour (a brand's, a place's), as Material's own tools do: palettes of its hue at every tone, as Android makes them from a wallpaper, then the roles from them. Each tone is the colour's CIELAB lightness, as in Material, so text keeps its contrast whatever the colour; the hues are worked in OKLCH, where they stay even. PalettesFromColour gives the palettes themselves. scheme.WithPrimary(…) puts a brand's colour in the primary roles only. scheme.Theme(dark) gives Go UI's own controls (its slider, text fields, menus) the scheme and sizes for fingers; set it as the context's theme before the pieces. ← All the documentation

guides/packaging.title: 📦 Packaging: go-ui-apk
guides/packaging.text: 📦 Packaging: go-ui-apk export ANDROID_HOME=…/android-sdk # with build-tools and a platform export ANDROID_NDK_HOME=…/ndk/<version> # and a JDK, 17 or later: javac on the path or in JAVA_HOME go run github.com/akrck02/go-ui-android/cmd/go-ui-apk -name Gallery -id io.example.gallery ./cmd/gallery It builds the program as a shared library for each processor asked for (arm64 phones by default) with the NDK's compiler (aligned to 16 KB pages, which Android 15 and later phones need), writes the manifest and a window theme that lets the program paint under the system's bars (light or dark with the phone) and beside a camera's cutout, compiles Go Renderer's two Java classes (what a screen reader reads, and the view the on-screen keyboard types in) with javac and the build tools' d8 , and packs, aligns and signs the package with the SDK's own aapt2 , zipalign and apksigner . The window shrinks while the on-screen keyboard is up. It signs with the debug key in ~/.android/debug.keystore , making it when missing, for phones and the emulator; a release is signed with the program's own key (below). Flag What it sets -name The name under the icon (required) -id The application id, like io.example.app (required) -o The package to write; the program's folder name .apk by default -version-code , -version The version's number and the version people read -min-sdk , -target-sdk The oldest Android it runs on (26, Android 8, at least) and the one it is made for -icon A square PNG for the launcher -icon-foreground , -icon-background , -icon-monochrome An adaptive icon, which each launcher cuts to its own shape: a PNG of 108 dp whose middle 66 dp always shows, a colour ( #rrggbb ) or a PNG behind it, and a one-colour PNG for themed icons (Android 13+) -splash , -splash-dark The colour ( #rrggbb ) the window shows while the program starts, in the light and the dark theme; Android 12 and later draw the icon over it -debuggable Lets adb read its folder and debug it; on by default -notifications Names the permission Android 13 and later ask before showing notifications -internet Lets the program use the network: on by default, granted when the package is installed with no question; -internet=false leaves it out -abi The processors to carry a library for: arm64 (phones, the default), x86_64 (the emulator on a PC), arm (old 32-bit phones); -abi arm64,x86_64 for several -release , -keystore , -key-alias Signs with the program's own key instead of the debug key, and leaves the package not debuggable: for a store -bundle With -release , writes an App Bundle ( .aab ), which Google Play asks for and makes each phone's packages from A release is signed with a key of the program's own, which a store knows it by from then on: keep the key store safe and out of the repository. The store's password is read from GO_UI_APK_STORE_PASSWORD (and the key's, when different, from GO_UI_APK_KEY_PASSWORD ), never from the command line, which other users of the computer can see: keytool -genkeypair -keystore lighthouses.keystore -alias lighthouses -keyalg RSA -validity 10000 GO_UI_APK_STORE_PASSWORD=… go run ./cmd/go-ui-apk -name Lighthouses -id io.example.lighthouses \ -release -keystore lighthouses.keystore -key-alias lighthouses -version-code 2 -version 1.1 ./cmd/lighthouses An App Bundle ( -bundle ) is what Google Play asks for: the same program, its resources in protocol buffers and its libraries in one base module, signed with the upload key; Play makes each phone's packages from it. Google's bundletool validates it and makes those packages to try on a phone ( bundletool build-apks --connected-device , then install-apks ); the gallery's bundle was tried that way on the emulator. What the program writes to its standard error (a panic, log.Fatal ) is in Android's log: adb logcat -s Go . ← All the documentation

guides/phone.title: 📱 Feeling at home on a phone
guides/phone.text: 📱 Feeling at home on a phone What a phone does that a desktop does not: fingers that swipe and hold, the back gesture, a screen that turns, notifications, and the phone's own services. Most of it comes from Go UI and Go Renderer; the pieces use it the way Android's own applications do. Gestures Go UI follows the one finger on a touch screen from where it comes down. Once it has moved a few pixels, the way it went first decides who takes it: the innermost list for up and down, the innermost of the sideways pieces (a carousel inside swiping pages) for sideways. The control it came down on is then not touched, and a finger that hardly moves stays a touch. So the pieces sit inside each other freely: the gallery has a carousel inside a list inside swiping pages, and rows swiped away inside a list pulled to refresh. Long press. A finger held still on a piece for half a second (Go UI's LongPressed ; with a mouse, its right button) long-presses it, and lifting it then is no touch. look.LongPressed() after a piece tells, and gives the phone's short buzz, as Android's own applications do. A list starts choosing with it: the row held is chosen ( Item.Selected ), touches choose more, and the top bar says how many, with a cross to stop ( TopBar.Close ) and actions for what is chosen. touched := look.ListItem("row", material.Item{Headline: light.name, Selected: light.chosen}) switch { case look.LongPressed(): light.chosen = true case touched && choosing: light.chosen = !light.chosen } Pull to refresh. The indicator follows the pull (Go UI's ScrollPull ); let go past 64 pixels, PullToRefresh returns true, and the program refreshes, keeping refreshing set until done. Swiping pages. A page let go past a third of the way, or flicked, turns to the next; the tab underline moves with the pages, between two tabs while a page is half way. Rows swiped away. Past two fifths of their width, or flicked, they go; short of that they slide back. Carousels. Let go, they glide on with the finger's speed and settle at a tile's edge. The stick. The finger that comes down on it holds it; Forward and Sideways go from -1 to 1. Other fingers stay free, so a program can turn a view with them ( context.Touches() , leaving out stick.Touching(touch) ). It can sit anywhere, in a Push scope, a list or swiping pages: the finger steering it is its own, so the pages and the list stay still under it. Back and motion A phone's back gesture reaches the program. Dialogs, sheets, the drawer and the floating menu answer it first and close; then look.Back() tells the screen, which stops choosing rows or goes back (to the first destination, to the list a detail came from). A back nobody answers sends the program to the background, as Android's own applications do at their first screen. Ask for it after drawing what goes over the screen, so that gets it first: defer func() { if screen != firstScreen && look.Back() { screen = firstScreen } }() Pieces move as Material's do, and only while they move does the window draw: the switch's handle slides and grows, the navigation bar's pill widens under the chosen icon, the tabs' underline slides, dialogs rise in as the screen darkens, sheets and the drawer slide in, the snackbar slides up, the floating menu's actions rise one after another, and look.Enter(key, …) lets a screen rise into place when it is first shown. They leave with motion too, though a program simply stops drawing them: a dialog answered fades out, a sheet slides back down, the drawer slides back off the side, the snackbar fades when its time is up, a side sheet slides back off its side, a floating menu's actions sink and fade as it closes, and a row's more folds back under it. Go UI keeps what such a layer painted last ( LayerOptions.Leave ) and lets that picture go; nothing in it can be touched on its way out. Turning the phone A phone on its side has more width than height to spare, and its camera's cutout at a side. Material moves the destinations from a bar at the bottom to a rail down the left: if look.Wide() { context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { look.NavigationRail(places, &screen) look.Body(true, func() { drawScreen(look) }) }) return } context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { look.Body(false, func() { drawScreen(look) }) look.NavigationBar(places, &screen) }) Body keeps the content clear of the cutout; go-ui-apk's window theme paints beside it ( shortEdges ), so no black strip is left there. Notifications A program's notifications go through Go UI's window: window.Notify(id, title, text) shows one in the phone's shade, even while the program is in the background, and touching it opens the program. Android 13 and later show them only once the person allows it: check window.NotificationsAllowed() and ask with window.AskForNotifications() when they do something that needs them. Build the package with go-ui-apk -notifications , which names the permission. In a browser they are the page's notifications; on the desktop they are not shown yet. The phone's services What a program asks of the phone goes through Go UI's window, and works in a browser too: Links and sharing. window.OpenLink(link) opens a web page in the browser, mailto: in the mail, tel: in the phone; window.Share(title, text) offers a text through the system's sheet. The gallery shares the lighthouses chosen in its list, and opens its project page from the menu. The clipboard. look.Context.Copy(text) puts a text on the phone's clipboard, and text fields copy and paste through it. Preferences. window.Preference(name) and window.KeepPreference(name, value) keep small values between runs. Android may end a program in the background without a word, so keep them in Options.Hidden , called when the program leaves the screen: the gallery keeps its screen, its theme and its colours there, and comes back as it was left. Sound. The feedback screen plays a note through Go Sound , which goes quiet when the gallery leaves the screen ( Options.Hidden ) and plays again when it comes back ( Options.Shown ). go-ui-apk passes the NDK's C++ compiler too, for the sound output's C++ (Oboe). The person's text size. Text grows with the phone's font size setting; icons and paddings keep theirs, as in Android's own applications. ← All the documentation

guides/pieces.title: 🧩 The pieces

sections.text: Gestures — gestures.go, and the stick — stick.go

guides/pieces.text: 🧩 The pieces Every piece, by Material's catalogue: navigation, actions, selection, inputs, containment, overlays, pickers, progress and gestures. The package's files follow the same order ( doc.go lists them). Navigation — navigation.go Piece What it is TopAppBar(TopBar{…}) The bar at the top, painted up under the status bar: a back arrow (a cross with Close , to leave a mode), a title and a subtitle, actions at its end; Large writes the title big under it, and with Scrolled (Go UI's ScrollOffset of the page under it) it shrinks into a small bar as the page goes up NavigationBar(destinations, &selected) Three to five destinations at the bottom, painted down under the gesture bar; Destination.Badge marks one with a count or a dot NavigationRail(destinations, &selected) The same down the left edge, on a wide screen ( Wide() ) NavigationDrawer(name, title, destinations, &selected) Every destination in a drawer sliding in from the left Tabs(name, labels, &selected) Primary tabs, the underline sliding to the one chosen TabPager(name, labels, &pager, page) Tabs over pages a finger swipes from side to side, the underline following them Body(besideRail, content) , Enter(key, content) A screen's content kept clear of the cutout and the gesture bar; a screen rising into place Navigation , Screens(name, &navigation, screen) , GoBack(&navigation) A stack of screens inside one place: Go(key) opens one sliding in from the right, GoBack from the system's back slides it away; the place's first screen is the key "" Back() , StatusBarScrim() The system's back for the screen (see Back and motion ); the strip under the status bar alone Actions — actions.go Piece What it is FilledButton , TonalButton , OutlinedButton , TextButton Actions, from the most to the least important; an icon before the label when given IconButton(icon) , RoundButton(icon, size, primary) A round 48-pixel target with an icon; a round button floating over a map or a scene FloatingButton(icon) , ExtendedFloatingButton(icon, label) The floating action button, alone or with its action written FloatingMenu(name, &menu) The floating action button opening into a few actions stacked above it; menu.Label names it for a screen reader SplitButton(icon, label) A main action joined to a button opening its other choices; tells which half was touched ButtonGroup(name, labels, &selected) Expressive's connected buttons: the chosen one fills and rounds out FloatingToolbar(name, tools, above) A pill of actions floating over the content at the bottom: an icon each, its label read by a screen reader Selection — selection.go and chips.go Piece What it is Switch(name, &on) , Checkbox(label, &on) , RadioButton(label, chosen) On or off; ticked or not; one of a few SegmentedButtons(name, options, &selected) Two to five choices sharing a row, one chosen Slider(name, &value, minimum, maximum, step) A value between two ends, dragged FilterChip(label, selected) , AssistChip(icon, label) , InputChip(label) A choice on or off in a row; an action suggested beside the content; something entered, with a cross to take it out Tag(text, ink, tint) A label in a pill of its own colours: a state, a count Inputs — inputs.go Piece What it is TextField(name, &text, Field{…}) Material's text field, outlined or Filled : a label, the box with a Prefix and a Suffix , a hint or an error under it and a Counter ; Secret with Reveal for a password and its eye. The on-screen keyboard comes up while it is typed in, suggests words and underlines the one it is composing; a finger held on a word selects it, with handles to drag and a bar to cut, copy and paste ( Look.Words in the person's language) Dropdown(name, label, choices, &dropdown) Material's exposed dropdown: a box showing the choice, opening the choices under it SearchView(name, placeholder, &search, content) A search pill that opens over the whole screen, ready to type in, with what the program finds under it SearchBar(name, &text, placeholder) A pill to search in, with a button to empty it Containment — containment.go Piece What it is ListItem(name, Item{…}) A list row: an icon in a round avatar (or a photo, Picture ), a headline, a supporting line, something at its end; Selected tints it and puts a tick in the avatar's place ExpandableItem(name, item, &open, more) A row that unfolds to show more under it and folds back, its chevron turning Card , ElevatedCard , OutlinedCard Containers for one subject: filled, raised over a scene, drawn by their border Avatar(name, icon, tint, size) , PictureAvatar(picture, size) A person's initials or a thing's icon in a circle; a photo in one Banner(icon, text, actions…) A message across the top of the content that stays until acted on SectionTitle , Heading , Divider A small heading over a list's rows; one for content with its own margins; a line between groups Text , Paragraph ( look.go ) One line; text that breaks into lines at the width it has Overlays — overlays.go Piece What it is Dialog(name, Dialog{…}) A question over the dimmed screen: an icon, a title, a text, more content, one or two actions. Returns Open , Confirmed or Dismissed BottomSheet(name, content) Choices or a short form in a sheet rising from the bottom StandardSheet(name, &sheet, peek, content) A sheet over the screen that does not dim it (a map's places): it rests low or expanded, and a finger drags it by its handle SideSheet(name, title, content) Filters or details in a sheet sliding in from the end, with a title and a cross Snackbar(&snackbar) A short note at the bottom for a few seconds, with an action ( snackbar.Show(text, action, duration) ) Menu(icon, choices) A button that opens a list of choices; returns the one chosen Pickers — pickers.go Piece What it is DatePicker(name, &picker, &date) A day chosen a month at a time, in a dialog; DateNames for another language TimePicker(name, &picker, &date) A time on Material's dial: the hours 1 to 12 round it and 13 to 00 inside, then the minutes; touched or dragged round Progress — progress.go Piece What it is LoadingIndicator(size) , ContainedLoadingIndicator(size) Expressive's indicator for a short wait: a filled shape turning and morphing from one form to the next, alone or on a round container CircularProgress(fraction, size, wavy) A ring filling as work gets done, or an arc chasing round ( Indeterminate ); wavy as Expressive draws it WavyProgress(fraction) , LinearProgress(fraction) A line filling with a travelling wave, a track and a stop dot; the plain line VideoPlayer(name, video, height) A film (Go UI's window.Video ) in a rounded box, a round play button over it while paused, a line of how far it has played; touching it plays or pauses Skeleton(width, height, radius) A quiet block with a light crossing it, standing in for content still coming Go Renderer draws rounded rectangles, shadows, text and icons; the indicators' shapes are made of rectangles in a box the program paints itself (Go UI's Context.Paint ): a shape is filled row by row and edged with small dots, a wave or an arc is a line of dots. An indicator asks for frames while it is on screen, and a screen without one sleeps: five of them at once take about a third of a core on a OnePlus 7 Pro, and nothing once the screen is left. Gestures — gestures.go, and the stick — stick.go Piece What it is LongPressed() Whether the piece drawn just before was held: the phone buzzes, and a list starts choosing rows PullToRefresh(name, refreshing, layout, rows) A list that refreshes when pulled down past its top and let go; the indicator stays while refreshing SwipeToDismiss(name, row) A row a finger slides away, a bin in the gap it leaves Carousel(name, &carousel, count, itemWidth, item) , CarouselItem A row of tiles slid sideways, gliding on and settling at a tile CarouselPicture(picture, height, title) A carousel item made of a photo, its title on a dark veil at its foot MultiBrowseCarousel(name, &carousel, count, largeWidth, height, item) Material's multi-browse carousel: large tiles, then a medium and a small one; tiles shrink towards the edges and grow as they come in Stick(name, &stick, size) An on-screen stick for walking or driving with a thumb Pictures Photos are Go Renderer's draw2d.Image : decode one once ( draw2d.DecodeImage reads a PNG, JPEG or GIF the program embeds) and keep it. context.Image(picture, layout, radius) draws it filling a box, cropped evenly where their shapes differ; the pieces take one where a photo belongs: Item.Picture in a list row's avatar, PictureAvatar , CarouselPicture in a carousel. The gallery paints its own pictures of a coast at different times of day, so it ships no photos. //go:embed north-cape.jpg var northCapeFile []byte northCape, err := draw2d.DecodeImage(bytes.NewReader(northCapeFile)) … look.ListItem("north", material.Item{Picture: northCape, Headline: "North Cape"}) Films window.OpenVideo(film) opens a film (the bytes of an MP4 or WebM, often embedded) and look.VideoPlayer shows it: on Android the phone's own decoders read it, in a browser the browser does, without sound for now; on the desktop films do not play yet ( window.ErrVideoUnsupported ). The gallery's film, six seconds of a made-up coast at dusk, plays in a card on the tabs screen; on a OnePlus 7 Pro it takes about two fifths of a core while it plays. //go:embed harbour.mp4 var harbour []byte video, err := window.OpenVideo(harbour) video.Loop = true … look.VideoPlayer("harbour", video, 180) ← All the documentation

guides/screen-readers.title: 🗣️ Screen readers
guides/screen-readers.text: 🗣️ Screen readers Every piece reads under TalkBack as Android's own do: a finger moved over the screen reads what is under it ("Lamp, switch, on"), a swipe goes to the next thing, a double tap presses it, and the thing read is ringed. Go UI works the list out from the boxes ( its docs ): a control is read by the texts inside it, texts side by side are read together, a list holds its rows, and what is behind a dialog or a sheet is left out. The pieces add what the boxes cannot tell: Piece Read as Switch , Checkbox , RadioButton A switch, a checkbox, a radio button, and whether it is on SegmentedButtons , ButtonGroup , a dropdown's choices, the date picker's days The chosen one selected NavigationBar , NavigationRail , Tabs Tabs, the one shown selected; a badge after the label TopAppBar , Dialog The title as a heading; the arrow as "Back" (or "Close") TextField The label over the box names the field, read with what is typed (not a secret one's); the screen reader's own typing, pasting and dictation fill it Slider Its range; the volume keys or a swipe up or down move it a step FloatingMenu , FloatingToolbar The menu's Label ("Create"), "Close" while open; each tool's label Icons with no label (a field's cross, the month's arrows, a Menu 's button, the split button's arrow) What they do ("More options"): Look.Words , English by default ( EnglishWords ) An icon button of the program's own reads its icon's name ("share 2") unless it has one: NamedIconButton("share-2", "Share") , or Describe after any piece. The gallery's test goes to every screen with double taps alone, and checks that every control has a name. The package carries one small Java class for it ( go-ui-apk compiles it in, see packaging ). It was tried on the Android 14 emulator with an accessibility service acting as TalkBack does: the gallery's tree reaches the system with every name, role and state, and a click goes to another destination, the focus rings a checkbox, a second click ticks it, a scroll moves the list on and text set on a field ("North light 🌊") lands in it whole. TalkBack itself, on a phone, is not tried yet. ← All the documentation

overview.title: Welcome to Go UI for Android 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go UI for Android 👋 Go UI for Android makes Android apps in Go that look and feel like Android's own : Material Design pieces (bars, lists, buttons, dialogs) and a tool that turns the program into an app you install on a phone. No Java, no Android Studio. You write the app once in Go with Go UI; the material pieces give it Android's looks (the wallpaper's colours, the back gesture, the on-screen keyboard), and go-ui-apk packs it into an .apk . The same program also opens on a computer, to try it as you go. Is it for me? ✅ You write Go and want an Android app . ✅ You want the app to feel at home on a phone : gestures, dark theme, TalkBack. ✅ You already know a little of Go UI . Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time just want to see every piece Try it without writing code 2 min are new and want the first lines Getting started 10 min want to learn step by step, up to a phone 🏴‍☠️ The quest : a lighthouse app, in 5 levels 90 min want to know about colours, gestures, screen readers or packaging The guides — want to use one piece (a top bar, a dialog, a carousel) Components : each one with real examples — are looking up a function The reference — Try it without writing code With Go installed and the projects copied (see Getting started ), the gallery shows every piece in a phone-sized window: go run ./cmd/gallery All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page Getting started Learn The quest : five levels, from a first screen to a phone Guides The pieces : the whole catalogue at a glance Colours Feeling at home on a phone Screen readers Packaging: go-ui-apk The gallery Use Components : every piece, one by one Reference The reference 🚧 Not done yet TalkBack itself, on a phone (see screen readers ). Keyboards for Chinese and Japanese (they compose as Android's own keyboard does, which is tried), right-to-left layout and Arabic letters joined, and emoji joined into one (a family, a skin tone): other scripts and colour emoji are drawn with the phone's own fonts. Sound in films: a film plays its pictures only (Go Sound plays other sounds). Words you will meet Word What it means Go A programming language. To try these projects you install it once, from go.dev, and type go run … in a terminal. Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. .apk file An Android app in one file, ready to install on a phone. Immediate mode A way of making interfaces: every moment the program describes the whole screen again from its data, so the screen can never show something out of date. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go UI for Android is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android (this one) Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

reference/material.title: material
reference/material.text: material import "github.com/akrck02/go-ui-android/material" Package material draws go-ui interfaces the way Android's own applications look (Material Design 3, with Material 3 Expressive's newer pieces). The pieces are made of go-ui boxes, texts and clickables, as any program can make controls of its own, so they draw the same on a phone, on a desktop and in a browser. A program makes a Look for each frame and calls its pieces: scheme := material.System(dark) // the wallpaper's colours on Android 12 and later context.Theme = scheme.Theme(dark) look := material.New(context, scheme) look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "Inbox"}) if look.FilledButton("plus", "New message") { … } The files follow Material's catalogue: look.go the Look, text and paragraphs scheme.go colour schemes: Material's baseline, a brand's colour dynamic.go the phone's wallpaper colours (Material You) theme.go go-ui's own controls in the scheme, and Roboto navigation.go top bars, the navigation bar, rail and drawer, tabs and swiping pages, the back actions.go buttons, floating buttons and their menu, split buttons, button groups, toolbars selection.go switches, check boxes, radio buttons, segmented buttons, sliders chips.go filter, assist and input chips, and tags inputs.go text fields and the search bar containment.go cards, list items, avatars, banners, section titles, dividers overlays.go dialogs, bottom sheets, snackbars, menus pickers.go date and time pickers progress.go loading indicators, circular, linear and wavy progress, skeletons gestures.go pull to refresh, rows swiped away, carousels stick.go an on-screen stick Functions Function func PalettesFromColour(seed draw2d.Color) window.Palettes PalettesFromColour makes the five palettes Android makes from a wallpaper, from one colour: the main one of its hue, a quieter one for the containers, a third of the hue turned a sixth of the way round, and two near-greys of its hue for the surfaces. func UseRoboto() UseRoboto draws every text in Roboto, Android's own typeface (SIL Open Font License, in fonts/). Constants and variables const Indeterminate = -1 Progress is how an indicator of known length shows its work: a fraction from 0 to 1, or Indeterminate for work of unknown length. const NavigationBarHeight = 80 NavigationBarHeight is a navigation bar's height without the gesture bar under it, for a snackbar or a floating button to keep above. var EnglishDates = DateNames{Title: "Select date", var EnglishTimes = TimeNames{Title: "Select time", Confirm: "OK", Dismiss: "Cancel"} EnglishTimes are the words a time picker shows by default. var EnglishWords = Words{Back: "Back", Close: "Close", Clear: "Clear", ShowPassword: "Show password", Answer Answer is what the person did with a dialog in a frame. type Answer int const ( Open Answer = iota // nothing yet: keep showing it Confirmed // the main action Dismissed // the other action, a touch outside, Escape ) Carousel Carousel is what a carousel remembers: where it rests, as the index of the first item shown. type Carousel struct { // Has unexported fields. } DateNames DateNames are the words a date picker shows, for a program in another language than English. type DateNames struct { Title string // over the date chosen Months [12]string // January first Weekdays [7]string // one or two letters each, Monday first Confirm string // the action that keeps the date Dismiss string // the one that leaves it } DatePicker DatePicker is what a date picker remembers while shown: the month on show and the day chosen. type DatePicker struct { Names DateNames // the zero value shows EnglishDates // Has unexported fields. } Destination Destination is a place the navigation bar leads to: an icon and a short label. type Destination struct { Icon, Label string // Badge marks the icon: a count ("3"), or a dot with "•"; none when empty. Badge string } Dialog Dialog is what a dialog says and offers. type Dialog struct { Icon string // over the title, centred; none when empty Title string Text string // under the title, broken into lines Content func() // more under the text (fields, choices); none when nil Confirm string // the main action, at the end Dismiss string // the other action, before it; none when empty } Dropdown Dropdown is what an exposed dropdown keeps: the choice, and whether its choices show. type Dropdown struct { Selected int // Has unexported fields. } Field Field is what a text field says around what is typed. type Field struct { Label string // above the box Placeholder string // in the box, quiet, while it is empty Supporting string // under the box: a hint Error string // under the box instead of the hint, in red, with the box red too MaxLength int // the most characters it takes; 0 = no limit // Counter shows how many characters there are of MaxLength, under the box at its end. Counter bool // Filled draws Material's filled field, a tinted box with a line under it, rather than the // outlined one: for a form on a plain screen, where boxes drawn by their border look empty. Filled bool // Prefix and Suffix are written in the box before and after what is typed: a currency, a unit. Prefix, Suffix string // Secret shows a dot for each character (a password). With Reveal, an eye at the box's end // shows the characters while *Reveal is true, and touching it turns *Reveal over. Secret bool Reveal *bool } FloatingMenu FloatingMenu is a floating action button that opens into a few related actions stacked above it, its icon turning into a cross. A program keeps one, and draws it with Look.FloatingMenu. type FloatingMenu struct { Icon string // the button's icon while closed Label string // what a screen reader reads for the button while closed ("Create") Actions []Destination // what it opens into: an icon and a label each // Above is how far over the bottom of the window it sits: a navigation bar's height // (NavigationBarHeight) when there is one. Above float32 Open bool } Item Item is what a list item shows. type Item struct { Icon string // in a round avatar at the start; none when empty Mark draw2d.Color // the avatar's colour; the primary container when zero // Picture is a photo in the round avatar instead of the icon (a person, a place). Picture *draw2d.Image Headline string Supporting string // the line under the headline; none when empty // Trailing draws what goes at the end (a Switch, an IconButton, a Tag); none when nil. Trailing func() // Selected marks the row chosen, in a list whose rows are chosen with a long press: it is tinted, // and a tick takes the avatar's place. Selected bool } Look Look draws the pieces in one frame, with one scheme. It is small: make one in every frame. Pieces that can be touched return true in the frame they are touched. Each takes the name go-ui tells it apart by: its label or icon, or a name given. Two pieces with the same name in one scope are one to go-ui: give repeated ones a scope each (ui.Context.Push). type Look struct { Context *ui.Context Scheme Scheme Words Words // the pieces' own words, in the person's language; the zero value is EnglishWords } Function or method func New(context *ui.Context, scheme Scheme) Look New makes the frame's Look. func (look Look) AssistChip(icon, label string) bool AssistChip suggests an action related to what is on screen (add to the calendar, share), with an icon before its label. func (look Look) Avatar(name, icon string, tint draw2d.Color, size float32) Avatar is a person or a thing shown in a circle: their initials (up to two letters of name) on a colour, or an icon when name is empty. func (look Look) Back() bool Back answers the system's back (a phone's back gesture) for the screen: true when there was one, and the program then goes back (to the first destination, to the list a detail came from). func (look Look) Banner(icon, text string, actions ...string) int Banner is a message across the top of the content that stays until acted on (no connection, an update to install), with an icon and one or two actions under its text. func (look Look) Body(besideRail bool, content func()) Body holds a screen's content between the bars: it grows to fill them and keeps its content clear of what the system draws at the sides (a camera's cutout, a navigation bar on the side). func (look Look) BottomSheet(name string, content func()) (dismissed bool) BottomSheet shows content in a sheet rising from the bottom of the screen, which is dimmed meanwhile: choices for what was touched, a short form. func (look Look) ButtonGroup(name string, labels []string, selected *int) bool ButtonGroup is a few choices joined side by side, than the screen, slid sideways with a finger: let go, it glides on with the finger's speed and settles at an item's edge. func (look Look) CarouselItem(height float32, tint draw2d.Color, icon, title string) CarouselItem is a carousel's usual item: a rounded tile in a colour, with a title over its foot. func (look Look) CarouselPicture(picture *draw2d.Image, height float32, title string) CarouselPicture is a carousel item made of a photo, with a title over its foot on a dark veil that keeps the title readable on any photo; an empty title leaves the photo alone (a narrow item). func float32, wavy bool) CircularProgress is a ring that fills as work gets done (fraction from 0 to 1), or, with Indeterminate, an arc chasing round. func (look Look) ContainedLoadingIndicator(size float32) ContainedLoadingIndicator is the indicator on a round container, to stand out over content (at the top of a list being refreshed). func (look Look) DatePicker(name string, picker *DatePicker, groups. func (look Look) Dropdown(name, label string, choices []string, dropdown *Dropdown) bool Dropdown is Material's exposed dropdown menu: a box like a text field's showing the choice, which opens the choices under it when touched. func (look Look) ElevatedCard(content func()) ElevatedCard is a card raised over what is beneath it: over a map or a scene. func (look Look) Enter(key string, content func()) Enter shows a screen rising gently into place when it is first shown, as Material's screens arrive: give each screen its own key. func (look Look) ExpandableItem(name string, item Item, open *bool, more func()) bool ExpandableItem is a list row that opens to show more under it (an answer under its question, the details of an order), its chevron turning. func (look Look) ExtendedFloatingButton(icon, label string) bool ExtendedFloatingButton is the floating action button with its action written beside the icon: clearer where the icon alone would not say it. func (look Look) FilledButton(icon, label string) bool FilledButton is the screen's main action, in the primary colour. func (look Look) FilterChip(label string, selected bool) bool FilterChip is a choice that square corners, raised over what scrolls beneath it. func (look Look) FloatingMenu(name string, menu *FloatingMenu) int FloatingMenu draws the button at the bottom end of the screen, over everything, and its actions while open. func (look Look) FloatingToolbar(name string, tools []Destination, above float32) int FloatingToolbar is a row of actions in a pill floating over the content at the bottom of the screen, for what is done to the content on show (edit, share, delete): each tool shows its icon, and a screen reader reads its label. func (look Look) GoBack(navigation *Navigation) bool GoBack answers the system's back by going back a screen, while there is one to go back to. func (look Look) Heading(text string) Heading is a section's small title in the primary colour, as SectionTitle, for 24-pixel icon, in the bars and beside list items. func (look Look) InputChip(label string) (touched, removed bool) InputChip is something the person entered or chose (a recipient, a tag), with a cross to take it out. func (look Look) LinearProgress(fraction float32) LinearProgress is a bar across that fills as work gets done: fraction from 0 to 1. func (look Look) ListItem(name string, item Item) bool ListItem is a row of a list, 72 pixels tall with a supporting line and 56 without. func (look Look) LoadingIndicator(size float32) LoadingIndicator is Material's indicator for a short wait of unknown length: a filled shape in the primary colour, turning and morphing from one form to the next. func (look Look) LongPressed() bool LongPressed tells whether the piece drawn just before it was long-pressed in this frame: a finger held still on it for half a second, or the mouse's right button. func (look Look) Menu(icon string, choices []string) int Menu is a button with an icon (three height float32, item func(index int, width float32)) MultiBrowseCarousel is Material's carousel for browsing many items at once: large items, then a medium one and a small one at the edge where the row runs off. func (look Look) NamedIconButton(icon, name string) bool NamedIconButton is an IconButton a screen reader (TalkBack) reads by a name, what it does ("Share"), rather than by its icon's. func (look Look) NavigationBar(destinations []Destination, selected *int) bool NavigationBar is the bar at the bottom, painted down under the gesture bar: three to five destinations, the selected one with its icon on a pill. func (look Look) NavigationDrawer(name, title string, destinations []Destination, selected *int) (closed bool) NavigationDrawer slides in from the left over the dimmed screen, navigation bar's form on a wide screen (a phone on its side, a tablet): the destinations down the left edge, painted under the status bar and beside a camera's cutout. func (look Look) OutlinedButton(icon, label string) bool OutlinedButton is a second action beside the main one. func (look Look) OutlinedCard(content func()) OutlinedCard is a card drawn by its border, among others on the surface. func (look Look) Paragraph(text string, size float32, weight draw2d.Weight, colour draw2d.Color) Paragraph writes text that breaks into lines at the width it has, word by word: a card's body, a description. func (look Look) PictureAvatar(picture *draw2d.Image, size float32) PictureAvatar is a person or a place shown by a photo in a circle. func (look Look) PullToRefresh(name string, refreshing bool, layout ui.Layout, content func()) (refresh bool) PullToRefresh is a scrolling list that refreshes when pulled down past its top and let go: a loading indicator follows the pull, and stays over the list while refreshing is true. func (look Look) RadioButton(label string, chosen bool) bool RadioButton is one of a few choices of which one is chosen, with a label after it. func (look Look) RoundButton(icon string, size float32, primary bool) bool RoundButton is a round floating button of any size, over a map or a scene (zoom in, zoom out, change the view). func (look Look) Screens(name string, navigation *Navigation, screen func(key string)) Screens draws the screen on top of a navigation: one gone to slides in from the end over the one it was gone to from, and slides back out when the program goes back. func (look Look) SearchBar(name string, text *string, placeholder string) bool SearchBar is a pill to search in, at the top of a screen. func (look Look) SearchView(name, placeholder string, search *Search, content func()) bool SearchView is Material's search: a pill at the top of a screen which, touched, opens over the whole screen ready to type in, with a way back and a cross to empty it; content shows under it what the program finds (the last searches, suggestions, results), and closes the search by setting search.Active to false when one is chosen. func (look Look) SectionTitle(text string) SectionTitle is a small heading over a group of rows, in the primary colour. func (look Look) SegmentedButtons(name string, options []string, selected *int) bool SegmentedButtons are two to five choices side by side sharing the row's width, one of them chosen (a view, a speed, a period). func (look Look) SideSheet(name, title string, content func()) (closed bool) SideSheet slides in from the end of the screen over the dimmed screen, headed by a title and a cross: filters for a list, the details of what is chosen, room for a form on a wide screen. func (look Look) Skeleton(width, height ui.Sizing, radius float32) Skeleton stands in for content still coming (a picture, a line of text): a quiet block with a light passing across it. func (look Look) Slider(name string, value *float32, minimum, maximum, step float32) bool Slider chooses a value between two ends by dragging, in steps (0 for any value): go-ui's slider in the
