the-quest/a-first-screen.title: Lesson 1: a first screen
the-quest/a-first-screen.text: Lesson 1: a first screen In this lesson you set the app up and draw its first screen: a large title, a list of lighthouses with a switch on each, and a floating button to add one. Mission Pieces Time The list, in a phone-sized window material.Look , schemes, TopAppBar , ListItem 15 min The idea Go UI is the pencil ; material is a stencil set cut to Android's own shapes: the same lines, but every bar, row and button comes out the size and colour Android's apps use, so the app feels at home on a phone. The module Clone Go UI for Android beside Go UI and Go Renderer (and Go Sound, which its gallery plays notes through), then make your module there: cd workspace git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-ui-android git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-sound mkdir lighthouses && cd lighthouses go mod init example.com/lighthouses for module in go-renderer go-ui go-ui-android go-sound; do go mod edit -require github.com/akrck02/$module@v0.0.0 -replace github.com/akrck02/$module=../$module done The data and main // lighthouse is the program's own data. type lighthouse struct { name, place string lit bool rangeNM float32 } // app is everything the program remembers between frames. type app struct { lighthouses []lighthouse place int // the destination chosen in the navigation bar navigation material.Navigation // the lighthouses' screens: "" is the list, a name its details removing string // the lighthouse the dialog asks about; "" when it is closed removed *lighthouse // the last one removed, for the note's Undo notes material.Snackbar dark bool ownColour bool // a teal of the app's own instead of the wallpaper's colours added int } // The destinations, in the navigation bar's order. const ( lighthousesPlace = iota settingsPlace ) var places = []material.Destination{{Icon: "lighthouse", Label: "Lighthouses"}, {Icon: "settings", Label: "Settings"}} func main() { options := window.Options{Title: "Lighthouses"} options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) flag.Parse() program := &app{ lighthouses: []lighthouse{ {name: "North Point", place: "On the northern cliffs", lit: true, rangeNM: 18}, {name: "East Cape", place: "At the end of the cape", lit: true, rangeNM: 12}, {name: "Harbour Mole", place: "At the harbour's mouth", rangeNM: 6}, {name: "South Reef", place: "On a rock off the reef", lit: true, rangeNM: 15}, }, dark: options.Dark || window.SystemPrefersDark(), } material.UseRoboto() // Android's typeface, before the window reads the fonts if err := window.Run(options, program.build); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } material.UseRoboto() draws every text in Roboto, Android's typeface; call it before the window opens. window.Options and RegisterFlags are Go UI's: -width 412 -height 892 gives the window a phone's size on the desktop, and -capture a picture. A frame with Material At every frame the program makes a scheme (Material's colour roles), gives Go UI's own controls its theme, and makes a material.Look , which draws the pieces: // build describes the app for this frame. func (program *app) build(context *ui.Context) { scheme := material.System(program.dark) // the wallpaper's colours on Android 12 and later if program.ownColour { scheme = material.FromColour(draw2d.Hex("#00796b"), program.dark) } context.Theme = scheme.Theme(program.dark) look := material.New(context, scheme) defer program.goBack(look) // last: what is over the screen answers the back first defer program.overlays(look) context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { look.Body(false, func() { switch program.place { case lighthousesPlace: look.Screens("lighthouses", &program.navigation, func(key string) { if key == "" { program.list(look) return } program.details(look, key) }) case settingsPlace: program.settings(look) } }) look.NavigationBar(places, &program.place) }) } For now leave out the two defer lines, the settings case and details (lessons 2 to 4), and draw the list without look.Screens . Body keeps the content clear of the camera's cutout and the gesture bar; NavigationBar comes in lesson 2. The list // list shows every lighthouse; touching one opens its screen. func (program *app) list(look material.Look) { context := look.Context look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "Lighthouses", Large: true}) context.ScrollArea("list", ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { for index := range program.lighthouses { light := &program.lighthouses[index] context.Push(light.name) icon := "lightbulb-off" if light.lit { icon = "lightbulb" } if look.ListItem("row", material.Item{Icon: icon, Headline: light.name, Supporting: light.place, Trailing: func() { look.Switch("lit", &light.lit) }}) { program.navigation.Go(light.name) } context.Pop() } }) context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(16), AlignX: ui.End}, func() { if look.ExtendedFloatingButton("plus", "New lighthouse") { program.added++ name := fmt.Sprint("New lighthouse ", program.added) program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses, lighthouse{name: name, place: "Not placed yet", rangeNM: 10}) program.navigation.Go(name) } }) } TopAppBar with Large writes the title big, as a screen's first level does on Android. ListItem is a Material row: an icon in a round avatar, a headline, a supporting line, and Trailing for what goes at its end. It returns true when touched. Rows repeat, so each gets a scope with context.Push (Go UI's ids). ExtendedFloatingButton is the floating action button with its action written. go run . -width 412 -height 892 The list on the desktop, in a phone's size Sizes are Material's: targets of at least 48 pixels, 16-pixel text. A finger has no hover, so pieces change only while pressed. Checkpoint In a 412 × 892 window: Lighthouses in large type, four rows with a bulb, a place and a switch, and New lighthouse floating at the bottom end. Achievement unlocked: Signwriter Bonus (optional) Show how many lighthouses are lit in the top bar's subtitle. ← Tutorial · Lesson 2: screens and the back gesture →

the-quest/colours-and-settings.title: Lesson 4: colours and settings
the-quest/colours-and-settings.text: Lesson 4: colours and settings Android 12 and later colour apps from the wallpaper (Material You). In this lesson the app does too, and a settings screen switches the dark theme and a colour of the app's own. Mission Pieces Time A settings screen System , FromColour , dark theme 10 min The idea On Android 12 and later, the phone paints every app with its wallpaper's colours , like a house where every room matches the hall. material.System asks for those colours; FromColour mixes a whole matching set from one colour of your own. Schemes Function Gives material.System(dark) The wallpaper's colours on Android 12+, Material's baseline elsewhere. Call it every frame: they change with the wallpaper material.Baseline(dark) Material's own purple material.FromColour(colour, dark) A whole scheme from one colour, as Material's tools make it scheme.WithPrimary(…) A brand's colour in the primary roles only scheme.Theme(dark) Go UI's theme from the scheme, for Go UI's own controls window.SystemPrefersDark() says whether the phone (or the desktop, or the browser) is in its dark theme. Lesson 1's build already picks the scheme from program.dark and program.ownColour . The settings screen // settings chooses the theme and the colours. func (program *app) settings(look material.Look) { look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "Settings", Large: true}) look.ListItem("dark", material.Item{Icon: "moon", Headline: "Dark theme", Trailing: func() { look.Switch("dark", &program.dark) }}) look.ListItem("colour", material.Item{Icon: "palette", Headline: "The app's own colour", Supporting: "Instead of the wallpaper's", Trailing: func() { look.Switch("colour", &program.ownColour) }}) } Settings in the dark theme, with the app's own teal To keep the choice between runs, use Go UI's window.KeepPreference in Options.Hidden , which is called when the app leaves the screen; Android may end it afterwards without a word ( feeling at home on a phone ). More in colours . Checkpoint On Settings , Dark theme darkens the app, and The app's own colour turns it teal; on a phone with Material You, the wallpaper's colours come back when it is off. Achievement unlocked: Painter The whole program // Command lighthouses is the go-ui-android tutorial's program: a phone app with a list of // lighthouses, a screen for each, a dialog before removing one, a note to undo it, and settings // for the theme and the colours. The same code runs on the desktop, in a web page and on Android. package main import ( "flag" "fmt" "log" "time" "github.com/akrck02/go-renderer/draw2d" ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" "github.com/akrck02/go-ui-android/material" "github.com/akrck02/go-ui/window" ) // lighthouse is the program's own data. type lighthouse struct { name, place string lit bool rangeNM float32 } // app is everything the program remembers between frames. type app struct { lighthouses []lighthouse place int // the destination chosen in the navigation bar navigation material.Navigation // the lighthouses' screens: "" is the list, a name its details removing string // the lighthouse the dialog asks about; "" when it is closed removed *lighthouse // the last one removed, for the note's Undo notes material.Snackbar dark bool ownColour bool // a teal of the app's own instead of the wallpaper's colours added int } // The destinations, in the navigation bar's order. const ( lighthousesPlace = iota settingsPlace ) var places = []material.Destination{{Icon: "lighthouse", Label: "Lighthouses"}, {Icon: "settings", Label: "Settings"}} func main() { options := window.Options{Title: "Lighthouses"} options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) flag.Parse() program := &app{ lighthouses: []lighthouse{ {name: "North Point", place: "On the northern cliffs", lit: true, rangeNM: 18}, {name: "East Cape", place: "At the end of the cape", lit: true, rangeNM: 12}, {name: "Harbour Mole", place: "At the harbour's mouth", rangeNM: 6}, {name: "South Reef", place: "On a rock off the reef", lit: true, rangeNM: 15}, }, dark: options.Dark || window.SystemPrefersDark(), } material.UseRoboto() // Android's typeface, before the window reads the fonts if err := window.Run(options, program.build); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // build describes the app for this frame. func (program *app) build(context *ui.Context) { scheme := material.System(program.dark) // the wallpaper's colours on Android 12 and later if program.ownColour { scheme = material.FromColour(draw2d.Hex("#00796b"), program.dark) } context.Theme = scheme.Theme(program.dark) look := material.New(context, scheme) defer program.goBack(look) // last: what is over the screen answers the back first defer program.overlays(look) context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { look.Body(false, func() { switch program.place { case lighthousesPlace: look.Screens("lighthouses", &program.navigation, func(key string) { if key == "" { program.list(look) return } program.details(look, key) }) case settingsPlace: program.settings(look) } }) look.NavigationBar(places, &program.place) }) } // list shows every lighthouse; touching one opens its screen. func (program *app) list(look material.Look) { context := look.Context look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "Lighthouses", Large: true}) context.ScrollArea("list", ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Height: ui.Grow()}, func() { for index := range program.lighthouses { light := &program.lighthouses[index] context.Push(light.name) icon := "lightbulb-off" if light.lit { icon = "lightbulb" } if look.ListItem("row", material.Item{Icon: icon, Headline: light.name, Supporting: light.place, Trailing: func() { look.Switch("lit", &light.lit) }}) { program.navigation.Go(light.name) } context.Pop() } }) context.Box(ui.Layout{Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(16), AlignX: ui.End}, func() { if look.ExtendedFloatingButton("plus", "New lighthouse") { program.added++ name := fmt.Sprint("New lighthouse ", program.added) program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses, lighthouse{name: name, place: "Not placed yet", rangeNM: 10}) program.navigation.Go(name) } }) } // details is a lighthouse's own screen. func (program *app) details(look material.Look, name string) { light := program.find(name) if light == nil { // removed while its screen was still sliding away return } if look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: light.name, Back: true, Actions: func() { if look.NamedIconButton("trash-2", "Remove") { program.removing = light.name } }}) { program.navigation.Back() } look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(16), Gap: 16}, func() { look.TextField("place", &light.place, material.Field{Label: "Where it stands", MaxLength: 60, Counter: true}) look.Slider("range", &light.rangeNM, 1, 30, 1) look.Text(fmt.Sprintf("Seen from %.0f nautical miles", light.rangeNM), 14, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurfaceVariant) look.Context.Row(func() { look.Text("Lit", 16, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurface) look.Context.Spacer() look.Switch("lit", &light.lit) }) }) } // settings chooses the theme and the colours. func (program *app) settings(look material.Look) { look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: "Settings", Large: true}) look.ListItem("dark", material.Item{Icon: "moon", Headline: "Dark theme", Trailing: func() { look.Switch("dark", &program.dark) }}) look.ListItem("colour", material.Item{Icon: "palette", Headline: "The app's own colour", Supporting: "Instead of the wallpaper's", Trailing: func() { look.Switch("colour", &program.ownColour) }}) } // overlays draws what goes over the screens: the dialog that asks before removing, and the note. func (program *app) overlays(look material.Look) { if program.removing != "" { answer := look.Dialog("remove", material.Dialog{Icon: "trash-2", Title: "Remove " + program.removing + "?", Text: "It leaves the list.", Confirm: "Remove", Dismiss: "Cancel"}) if answer == material.Confirmed { program.remove(program.removing) program.navigation.Back() program.notes.Show(program.removed.name+" removed", "Undo", 5*time.Second) } if answer != material.Open { program.removing = "" } } program.notes.Above = material.NavigationBarHeight if look.Snackbar(&program.notes) && program.removed != nil { program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses, *program.removed) // Undo program.removed = nil } } // goBack answers the system's back: from a lighthouse to the list, from settings to the list; // from the list nobody answers, and the app goes to the background. func (program *app) goBack(look material.Look) { if program.place == lighthousesPlace && look.GoBack(&program.navigation) { return } if program.place != lighthousesPlace && look.Back() { program.place = lighthousesPlace } } func (program *app) find(name string) *lighthouse { for index := range program.lighthouses { if program.lighthouses[index].name == name { return &program.lighthouses[index] } } return nil } func (program *app) remove(name string) { for index, light := range program.lighthouses { if light.name == name { program.removed = &light program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses[:index], program.lighthouses[index+1:]...) return } } } ← Lesson 3 · Lesson 5: on a phone →

the-quest/fields-dialogs-and-notes.title: Lesson 3: fields, dialogs and notes
the-quest/fields-dialogs-and-notes.text: Lesson 3: fields, dialogs and notes In this lesson a lighthouse's screen edits it, a dialog asks before removing it, and a note at the bottom offers to undo. Mission Pieces Time Editing, removing and undoing TextField , Slider , Dialog , Snackbar 15 min The idea A dialog is a question that needs an answer before anything else happens; a snackbar is a sticky note on the fridge: it says what just happened and offers to take it back, and falls off by itself after a few seconds. Editing Lesson 2's details already has the pieces: Piece Edits TextField(name, &text, material.Field{Label, Placeholder, Supporting, Error, MaxLength, Counter, Filled, Prefix, Suffix, Secret, Reveal}) A string. On a phone the on-screen keyboard comes up, suggests words and underlines the one it composes; a held word is selected, with handles and a bar to cut, copy and paste Slider(name, &value, minimum, maximum, step) A number Switch(name, &on) A bool Dropdown , SegmentedButtons , Checkbox , RadioButton , DatePicker , TimePicker See the pieces A dialog Dialog(name, material.Dialog{…}) is a question over the dimmed screen. Show it while your program wants (here, while removing names a lighthouse); it returns material.Open while it waits, then Confirmed or Dismissed (the other button, a touch outside, or the back gesture) once. A note with Undo A material.Snackbar is kept by the program: Show(text, action, duration) when something happens, and look.Snackbar(&snackbar) at every frame, which returns true when its action is touched. Above lifts it over the navigation bar. // overlays draws what goes over the screens: the dialog that asks before removing, and the note. func (program *app) overlays(look material.Look) { if program.removing != "" { answer := look.Dialog("remove", material.Dialog{Icon: "trash-2", Title: "Remove " + program.removing + "?", Text: "It leaves the list.", Confirm: "Remove", Dismiss: "Cancel"}) if answer == material.Confirmed { program.remove(program.removing) program.navigation.Back() program.notes.Show(program.removed.name+" removed", "Undo", 5*time.Second) } if answer != material.Open { program.removing = "" } } program.notes.Above = material.NavigationBarHeight if look.Snackbar(&program.notes) && program.removed != nil { program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses, *program.removed) // Undo program.removed = nil } } func (program *app) remove(name string) { for index, light := range program.lighthouses { if light.name == name { program.removed = &light program.lighthouses = append(program.lighthouses[:index], program.lighthouses[index+1:]...) return } } } The dialog before East Cape is removed overlays is deferred in build , so it is drawn over the screens and answers the back before them. Checkpoint The bin on a lighthouse's screen asks Remove East Cape? ; Remove takes it out, goes back to the list and shows East Cape removed with Undo , which puts it back. Achievement unlocked: Lamplighter Bonus (optional) Give the field an error, "A place is needed", while it is empty. ← Lesson 2 · Lesson 4: colours and settings →

the-quest/on-a-phone.title: Lesson 5: on a phone
the-quest/on-a-phone.text: Lesson 5: on a phone The app runs on the desktop. In this lesson it becomes an Android package, installed on an emulator or your own phone. You need no Java code, Gradle or Android Studio: go-ui-apk builds the program with the NDK and packs it with the SDK's own tools. Mission Pieces Time The app installed the SDK, the NDK, go-ui-apk, adb 30 min The idea go-ui-apk is a removal company : it packs your program (built for the phone's processor with the NDK), Android's paperwork (the manifest, the icon) and a signature into one box, the .apk , which the phone unpacks and installs. 1. Install the Android tools You need Why How The Android SDK command-line tools, with platform-tools , build-tools and a platforms;android-… aapt2 , zipalign , apksigner , d8 and adb developer.android.com/studio#command-tools , then sdkmanager "platform-tools" "build-tools;35.0.0" "platforms;android-35" The NDK Compiles the Go program (cgo) for the phone's processor sdkmanager "ndk;27.2.12479018" A JDK 17 or later Compiles Go Renderer's two small Java classes (the screen reader's, the keyboard's) javac on the PATH , or JAVA_HOME export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/android-sdk export ANDROID_NDK_HOME=$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/27.2.12479018 2. Build the package From the app's folder: go run github.com/akrck02/go-ui-android/cmd/go-ui-apk -name Lighthouses -id io.example.lighthouses . -name is the name under the icon, -id the application id (a reversed domain you own). It writes lighthouses.apk , signed with the debug key ( ~/.android/debug.keystore , made when missing), for arm64 phones. For the emulator on a PC add -abi arm64,x86_64 . 3. Install it On a phone: turn on Developer options and USB debugging , plug it in, then adb install lighthouses.apk Or on an emulator: make one with avdmanager (an x86_64 system image), start it with emulator -avd <name> , and adb install the same way. What the program writes to standard error (a panic, log.Print ) is in Android's log: adb logcat -s Go window.LastCrash() gives the program the report of its last crash, to show or send. 4. Make it look finished Flag Gives -icon-foreground fg.png -icon-background '#00796b' -icon-monochrome mono.png An adaptive icon, cut to each launcher's shape, and a themed one -splash '#fef7ff' -splash-dark '#141218' The window's colour while the app starts -notifications The permission Android 13+ asks before window.Notify -version-code 2 -version 1.1 The version 5. A release A store knows an app by its key: make one, keep it safe and out of the repository, and pass its password through the environment, never the command line: keytool -genkeypair -keystore lighthouses.keystore -alias lighthouses -keyalg RSA -validity 10000 GO_UI_APK_STORE_PASSWORD=… go run github.com/akrck02/go-ui-android/cmd/go-ui-apk \ -name Lighthouses -id io.example.lighthouses \ -release -keystore lighthouses.keystore -key-alias lighthouses -bundle . -bundle writes the App Bundle ( .aab ) Google Play asks for. Every flag is in packaging . Checkpoint adb install lighthouses.apk says Success ; the app is in the phone's launcher, opens on the list, and adb logcat -s Go shows what it prints. Achievement unlocked: Shipper What you learnt go-ui-apk turns a Go main package into an .apk with the SDK, the NDK and a JDK. adb install and adb logcat -s Go for trying and debugging. Releases are signed with your own key; -bundle for Google Play. Final challenge · Lighthouse network Turn the phone on its side: the app should move its destinations from the bar at the bottom to a rail down the left, as Android's own apps do on a wide screen. Hint: look.Wide() says the screen has more width than height to spare; NavigationRail takes the same destinations as the bar, and look.Body(true, …) keeps the content beside it. Try it on your own first, then compare with the solution. The final challenge: the app on its side, the destinations on a rail down the left Rare achievement unlocked: Lighthouse network Well done Every achievement of the quest Where next The pieces : every Material piece, with pictures. Feeling at home on a phone : gestures, turning the phone, notifications, services. Screen readers : how TalkBack reads the app. The gallery : every piece in one program, to read its code. The reference . ← Lesson 4 · Tutorial

the-quest/screens-and-back.title: Lesson 2: screens and the back gesture
the-quest/screens-and-back.text: Lesson 2: screens and the back gesture A phone app moves between screens: destinations at the bottom, and inside one a stack of screens, each sliding in over the one before. In this lesson the app gets both, and answers the system's back gesture as Android's own apps do. Mission Pieces Time A screen for each lighthouse NavigationBar , Navigation , Screens , GoBack 20 min The idea Screens stack like plates : opening a lighthouse puts its screen on top, and the back gesture takes the top plate off. The navigation bar picks which pile you look at. Destinations NavigationBar(destinations, &selected) draws three to five destinations at the bottom, under the gesture bar; it changes selected when one is touched: var places = []material.Destination{{Icon: "lighthouse", Label: "Lighthouses"}, {Icon: "settings", Label: "Settings"}} build shows the destination chosen with a switch , then the bar (lesson 1's build ). On a phone turned on its side, look.Wide() is true: draw NavigationRail down the left instead, with look.Body(true, …) ( feeling at home on a phone ). A stack of screens A material.Navigation is a stack of screen names, kept by the program. Go(name) opens one, sliding in from the right; Back() returns. look.Screens draws the one on top, by its name: "" is the first. look.Screens("lighthouses", &program.navigation, func(key string) { if key == "" { program.list(look) return } program.details(look, key) }) The list's rows call program.navigation.Go(light.name) . A lighthouse's screen has a top bar with a back arrow; TopAppBar returns true when it is touched: // details is a lighthouse's own screen. func (program *app) details(look material.Look, name string) { light := program.find(name) if light == nil { // removed while its screen was still sliding away return } if look.TopAppBar(material.TopBar{Title: light.name, Back: true, Actions: func() { if look.NamedIconButton("trash-2", "Remove") { program.removing = light.name } }}) { program.navigation.Back() } look.Context.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Width: ui.Grow(), Padding: ui.Pad(16), Gap: 16}, func() { look.TextField("place", &light.place, material.Field{Label: "Where it stands", MaxLength: 60, Counter: true}) look.Slider("range", &light.rangeNM, 1, 30, 1) look.Text(fmt.Sprintf("Seen from %.0f nautical miles", light.rangeNM), 14, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurfaceVariant) look.Context.Row(func() { look.Text("Lit", 16, draw2d.Regular, look.Scheme.OnSurface) look.Context.Spacer() look.Switch("lit", &light.lit) }) }) } A lighthouse's screen The back gesture Android's back gesture reaches the program. Dialogs, sheets and drawers answer it first and close. Then the screen: look.GoBack(&navigation) goes back a screen when there is one, and look.Back() takes the back for anything else. A back nobody takes sends the app to the background, as at a phone app's first screen. Ask last in the frame, after what goes over the screens, so that gets it first. build does it with defer : // goBack answers the system's back: from a lighthouse to the list, from settings to the list; // from the list nobody answers, and the app goes to the background. func (program *app) goBack(look material.Look) { if program.place == lighthousesPlace && look.GoBack(&program.navigation) { return } if program.place != lighthousesPlace && look.Back() { program.place = lighthousesPlace } } Checkpoint Touching North Point slides its screen in from the right; the arrow, or the phone's back gesture, slides it away; Settings in the bar opens the other destination. Achievement unlocked: Pathfinder Bonus (optional) Make the settings destination a stack too, with an "About" row that opens an "About" screen. ← Lesson 1 · Lesson 3: fields, dialogs and notes →

the-quest/the-quest.title: Tutorial: a lighthouse app for phones
the-quest/the-quest.text: Tutorial: a lighthouse app for phones The quest map: Signwriter, Pathfinder, Lamplighter, Painter, Shipper, then the final challenge, Lighthouse network In five lessons you build an Android app in Go that looks and behaves like Android's own: a list of lighthouses, a screen for each, a dialog before removing one, a note to undo it, settings for the theme and the colours, and the back gesture. You try it on the desktop as you go, and end with it installed on a phone. Before you start , know Go UI's basics: its Get started and, better, the first lessons of its tutorial . This tutorial uses the same immediate mode, with Material pieces instead of Go UI's own. Every lesson has the same shape, as in a quest: the idea in everyday words, the code , a checkpoint to know it works, a bonus with its solution folded, and an achievement to unlock. A final challenge waits at the end of lesson 5. Lesson You learn You end with 1. A first screen material.Look , schemes, the top bar, list items, the floating button The list, in a phone-sized window 2. Screens and the back gesture The navigation bar, a stack of screens, GoBack , Back A screen for each lighthouse 3. Fields, dialogs and notes Text fields, sliders, switches, Dialog , Snackbar Editing, removing and undoing 4. Colours and settings The wallpaper's colours, a scheme from one colour, the dark theme A settings screen 5. On a phone The SDK, the NDK, go-ui-apk, the emulator, the log, a release The app installed The whole program is at the end of lesson 4 . ← Documentation · Lesson 1 →
